title: Aeroflot 1668
summary: The flight departed Olyokminsk at 18:10 in good weather. At 18:24, radar showed the aircraft at 4,500 meters 75 kilometers from Olyokminsk. At 18:28, radar contact was lost. The aircraft was found crashed the next day with both wings and empennage separated from fuselage due to high aerodynamic loads. The aircraft was in an 80 degree nose-down attitude at impact. The exact cause could not be determined but may have involved flight control or structural failure.
probable_cause: Unable to determine exact cause. The aircraft suddenly entered a steep dive with both wings and empennage separating from fuselage due to high aerodynamic loads.

factors.evidence: aircraft was in an 80 degree nose down attitude at 18:27
theory was that an aircraft flight control system failed, causing sudden steep descent
investigation could not determine root cause, suggesting possible design or structural vulnerability

Radar contact with aircraft was lost and attempts to communicate by radio were unsuccessful; aircraft was in 80 degree nose-down attitude on heading 270 with left bank
Aircraft struck trees then crashed heavily with both wings and empennage separated from fuselage due to high aerodynamic loads

notes: true cause undetermined; investigation unable to identify mechanism

title: 1968 Indian Air Force An-12 crash
summary: Indian Air Force An-12 Flight 203, flown by Flight Lieutenant Harkewal Singh and Squadron Leader Pran Nath Malhotra, was on approach to Leh from Chandigarh when the pilot turned back due to inclement weather; the aircraft went missing with its last radio contact over the Rohtang Pass and was declared lost after searches failed to find the wreck. Expeditions between 2003 and 2024 have recovered remains and wreckage from Himalayan glaciers, confirming the aircraft went down in terrain at about 18,000 ft.

factors.evidence: the pilot decided to turn back due to inclement weather
the aircraft then went missing with the last radio contact over the Rohtang Pass
The crash location lies at a height of about 18,000 ft, at a gradient of 80 degrees

events.text: Flight 203 was on approach to Leh when the pilot decided to turn back due to inclement weather.
The aircraft went missing, with the last radio contact over the Rohtang Pass, and was declared missing after the failure to find the wreck.
On 18 August 2019, a joint Indian Army and Air Force team recovered aircraft parts including the aero engine, fuselage, propeller and a cockpit door.

notes: No formal investigation finding stated; aircraft was missing for decades, only wreckage/remains recovered.

title: Aeroflot 15
summary: Aircraft at cruise altitude of 8,000 meters developed an emergency forcing sudden descent at 22:38 local time. Crew attempted pitch correction but unintentionally pitched further down, causing overspeed. Aircraft became inverted at 1,000 meters altitude. Investigation found evidence of engine 3 malfunction and left wing fuel leak but rejected fire theory and concluded exact cause unknown.

factors.evidence: engine number three did not perform as expected
crew unintentionally pitched the aircraft further down to the point of overspeed while trying to correct the pitch
left wing showed evidence of a fuel leak
aircraft inverted and broke apart at 1000 meters altitude

events.text: At 22:37 local time the flight crew switched communications to Bratsk air traffic control, reporting altitude of 8,000 meters and cruising speed of 780 km/h.
At 22:38:38 the airliner was forced into sudden descent as engine number three did not perform as expected.
At 22:41:28 the situation evolved into a full emergency as the crew unintentionally pitched the aircraft further down to the point of overspeed while trying to correct the pitch.
At 22:43:12 at an altitude of 3,000 meters air traffic controllers detected a short unintelligible transmission from the flight determined to be about the state of the aircraft.
At 22:43:47 the airliner began to break apart at 1,000 meters altitude at a speed of 890 km/h and crashed 13 kilometers away from Parchum.

title: Air France 212 (1968)
summary: Air France Flight 212, a Boeing 707 on a scheduled service from Santiago to Paris, crashed on 6 March 1968 while approaching Le Raizet Airport in Pointe-à-Pitre, Guadeloupe. The aircraft was cleared for a visual approach and began descent from 9,000 feet, but struck Grande Découverte mountain at 3,937 feet, killing all 63 occupants. Accident investigators determined the probable cause was initiation of a nighttime visual approach from an incorrectly identified point.
probable_cause: Initiation of a nighttime visual approach from an incorrectly identified point

title: Aer Lingus 712
summary: Flight 712 crashed into the sea off Tuskar Rock, County Wexford, on March 24, 1968, killing all 61 passengers and crew. The aircraft was proceeding normally until a call was heard with probable contents twelve thousand feet descending spinning rapidly; thereafter no further radio contact was established. Investigation lasted two years but a definitive cause was never determined. A 2002 review concluded the crash was likely caused by a chain of events starting with flutter-induced fatigue failure of the elevator trim tab mechanism, though other theories including bird strike or structural failure from corrosion were also proposed.
probable_cause: Likely consequence of a chain of events starting with a failure to the left tail-plane caused by metal fatigue, corrosion, flutter, or a bird strike, with the most likely cause being a flutter-induced fatigue failure of the elevator trim tab operating mechanism.

title: South African Airways 228
summary: South African Airways Flight 228, a new Boeing 707 taking off from Windhoek on 20 April 1968 in a dark, moonless night with no ground lights, initially climbed to 650 ft then leveled off and started to descend. Fifty seconds after takeoff the aircraft flew into terrain at approximately 271 knots. The crew failed to maintain safe airspeed and altitude by not observing flight instruments.
probable_cause: The captain and first officer failed to maintain a safe airspeed and altitude and a positive climb by not observing flight instruments during takeoff. Loss of situational awareness in dark, moonless night conditions contributed; the crew misread altitude and vertical speed indicators.

factors.evidence: It was a dark, moonless night with few, if any, lights on the ground in the open desert

events.text: The aircraft took off from Windhoek on runway 08 at 18:49 GMT into a dark, moonless night.
The aircraft initially climbed to an altitude of 650 ft above ground level, then leveled off.

Fifty seconds after take-off, the aircraft flew into the ground in flight configuration at approximately 271 knots.
The aircraft's four engines were the first parts to touch the ground, creating four deep gouges in the soil.
Two fires erupted immediately when the aircraft's fuel tanks ignited.

title: Braniff 352
summary: Braniff Flight 352, a Lockheed L-188A Electra, departed Houston for Dallas on May 3, 1968, climbing to 20,000 feet. About 25 minutes into the flight, the crew encountered severe thunderstorm activity with hail. The crew requested and received clearance for a 180-degree right turn to escape the weather. During the turn, the aircraft's bank angle exceeded 90 degrees and the nose pitched down 40 degrees, producing a peak acceleration of 4.3g that exceeded the airframe's ultimate structural strength. The aircraft broke apart in flight, killing all 85 occupants.
probable_cause: The stressing of the aircraft structure beyond its ultimate strength during an attempted recovery from an unusual attitude induced by turbulence associated with a thunderstorm. The operation in the turbulence resulted from a decision to penetrate an area of known severe weather.

factors.evidence: The aircraft approached an area of severe thunderstorm activity with hail reported in the area at 16:47.
During the requested 180-degree turn, the aircraft's bank angle was increased to more than 90 degrees and the nose pitched down to about 40 degrees.
The FDR indicated a peak acceleration of 4.3 g, which caused overstress to the airframe and resulted in its breakup.
The aircraft went into an uncontrolled descent after structural failure occurred.

events.text: Departed William P. Hobby Airport at FL200 for Dallas Love Field.

Requested descent to 5,000 feet and asked ATC if hail had been reported in the area.

title: 1968 Kham Duc C-130 shootdown
summary: A USAF C-130B commanded by Major Bernard L. Bucher was shot down on 12 May 1968 while evacuating civilians from the besieged Kham Duc camp. After landing under fire and loading 150 evacuees, Bucher took off northward, unaware North Vietnamese forces were concentrated there; under fire from 12.7mm and 14.5mm heavy machine guns the aircraft shook violently out of control and crashed into a ravine less than a mile from the airstrip, killing everyone aboard.

title: Air France 1611
summary: Air France Flight 1611, a Sud Aviation Caravelle, took off from Ajaccio at 10:09 on 11 September 1968, bound for Nice. The flight was initially without incident and weather conditions were sunny. At 10:30 local time, on descending between flight level 90 to flight level 70, the flight crew declared an emergency mentioning a fire on board. The radio and radar contact was lost after a final contact at 10:33, and a kerosene slick and floating debris were discovered, confirming that the plane had crashed into the sea with all 95 people aboard.
probable_cause: The report surmised that the loss of the aircraft was caused by a fire in the passenger toilet caused either by a defective water heater or a cigarette discarded in a waste bin. The direct cause of loss of control could not be definitively established: it may be related to the pilots' physical incapacity caused either by toxic gas emissions or by passengers invading the cockpit.

title: Northeast Airlines 946
summary: Flight 946 crashed on approach to Lebanon Municipal Airport while descending on a standard approach during instrument conditions with an estimated ceiling of 2,000 feet overcast. The aircraft struck Moose Mountain at approximately 2,237 feet altitude, about 600 feet below the required minimum altitude of 2,800 feet. The NTSB determined that the pilots prematurely started their descent and were unable to accurately determine their position, with no supplemental navigational aids available at the airport.
probable_cause: Pilots prematurely started their descent and were not able to accurately determine their position as they had performed a nonstandard approach and there were no supplemental navigational aids available for their use.

factors.evidence: Weather was an estimated ceiling of 2,000 feet overcast with visibility of 10 miles.

events.text: Northeast Airlines Flight 946 departed Logan International Airport at 5:42 p.m. ET with 39 passengers and three crew.
At 6:11 p.m., the pilots radioed that they were executing a standard approach maneuver before preparing to land.
The aircraft was flying at approximately 2,237 feet altitude when it should have been no lower than 2,800 feet.
At approximately 6:17 p.m., the plane crashed into the side of Moose Mountain; 31 people died on impact and one died later.

notes: Cockpit voice recorder badly damaged; no CVR data available

title: Wien Consolidated Airlines 55
summary: Fairchild F-27B Flight 55 was at 11,500 ft preparing to approach Iliamna when it encountered extreme turbulence. The aircraft had fatigue cracks in its wings from improper and shoddy maintenance that could not withstand the stresses. The structural failure of the right wing forced the aircraft into a steep, uncontrolled spiral descent that crashed into Pedro Bay.

title: Pan Am 217
summary: Pan Am Flight 217, a Boeing 707, crashed into the Caribbean Sea near Caracas at 22:05 local time while nearing Caracas on approach from New York. The crew was caught by an optical illusion created by the lights of the city on an upslope. All 51 passengers and crew perished. The aircraft disappeared from radar and crashed into the Caribbean Sea, with wreckage found 11.4 miles from Caracas.
probable_cause: Pilot error resulting from an optical illusion created by the lights of the city of Caracas on an upslope caused the crew to descend until they crashed into the sea.

title: Allegheny Airlines 736
summary: Flight 736 was approaching Bradford Regional Airport in a blinding snowstorm with one-mile visibility when both pilots focused outside the cockpit trying to establish visual reference to the runway. The aircraft continued descending below the minimum descent altitude of 2,543 feet and struck trees 462 feet below this altitude, about 2.1 nautical miles short of the runway. The aircraft rolled inverted and broke apart. The investigation found that minimal visual references at night, a small navigational error, and rapid worsening of visibility conditions contributed to the descent below minimums.
probable_cause: Continuation of descent from the final approach fix through the Minimum Descent Altitude and into obstructing terrain at a time when both flight crewmembers were looking outside the aircraft in an attempt to establish visual reference to the ground. Contributing factors were the minimal visual references available at night on the approaches to the Bradford Regional Airport; a small but critical navigational error during the later stages of the approach; and a rapid change in visibility conditions that was not known to the crew.

title: North Central Airlines 458
summary: During a night approach to O'Hare in 200-foot ceilings and light rain, at 210 feet the CV-580 began climbing. The captain initiated a go-around but the aircraft continued climbing and stalled. It rolled left, struck the ground, and crashed into a hangar. The NTSB determined the captain experienced spatial disorientation from atmospheric refraction of approach lights at a critical moment when transitioning between instrument and visual reference.
probable_cause: Spatial disorientation of the captain caused by atmospheric refraction of approach lights during transition from instrument to visual flight reference, combined with relatively low command experience in the CV-580.

title: MacRobertson Miller Airlines 1750
summary: Vickers Viscount Flight 1750 was descending from 19,000 ft to Port Hedland when half the right wing separated in flight at 7,000 ft on descent. Investigation found metal fatigue in the wing spar's lower boom with cracks affecting 85 percent of the cross-section, initiated by improper maintenance of a bush that broached the hole and removed the interference fit. The outer half-wing and engine separated, and the fuselage struck the ground 26 seconds later.
probable_cause: Metal fatigue in the right wing's lower boom caused structural failure and in-flight separation of the outer half-wing. The fatigue was initiated at a bolt hole where improper maintenance actions years earlier had scored the hole and removed the interference fit of a structural bush, reducing fatigue resistance.
